part_title: ENA, EFA, HPC and Auto Scaling Capacity

scenes.title: ENI performance: ENA versus EFA
scenes.visual_overview: The approved SAP slide diagrams eni performance: ena versus efa in four numbered visual sections and a remember takeaway.
visual_walkthrough: Inspect ENA enhanced network adapter for ordinary supported EC2 workloads
Compare EFA low-latency OS-bypass supported HPC/ML workloads
Explain EFA software and placement requirements and security groups
Measure throughput, packet rate and latency rather than relying on advertised bandwidth
scenes.visual_example: Review a production compute workload against the diagram and evaluate its concrete performance, security and failure requirements.
scenes.visual_synthesis: The architecture is appropriate only after its operational requirements, limits and failure response are validated.
scenes.narration: This slide shows two network options with different workload goals. Begin with the cyan left panel, the Elastic Network Adapter, or ENA. It enables enhanced networking on supported EC2 instances and is appropriate for many ordinary network-intensive services. The performance you get still depends on the instance type, network limits and configuration. Now inspect the purple EFA panel. Elastic Fabric Adapter is designed for suitable tightly coupled high performance computing and machine-learning workloads, where supported libraries can use low-latency communication. EFA's OS-bypass communication requires compatible software and deployment conditions, including appropriate placement and security settings. It is not an automatic speed boost for every web server. The four callouts at the bottom turn the comparison into a decision. Determine whether the workload needs enhanced standard networking or specialized tightly coupled communication, confirm instance and software support, and benchmark the actual traffic pattern. Compare packet rate, latency, network throughput and application behavior. A larger headline bandwidth number does not resolve bottlenecks in storage, CPU or application scheduling. Choose ENA for general enhanced networking, and EFA when the supported HPC communication pattern justifies it.

scenes.title: HPC: the slowest layer limits the job
scenes.visual_overview: The approved SAP slide diagrams hpc: the slowest layer limits the job in four numbered visual sections and a remember takeaway.
visual_walkthrough: Compare tightly coupled jobs with independent jobs and inter-node communication requirements
Read storage access patterns for durable objects, shared files, blocks and local scratch
Trace FSx for Lustre integration and data staging with S3
Evaluate batch scheduling, ParallelCluster tooling, checkpoints and job recovery
scenes.visual_example: Review a production compute workload against the diagram and evaluate its concrete performance, security and failure requirements.
scenes.visual_synthesis: The architecture is appropriate only after its operational requirements, limits and failure response are validated.
scenes.narration: This slide asks you to optimize the whole high performance computing workload rather than one headline compute specification. On the upper left, tightly coupled jobs exchange messages frequently between nodes. Their performance can suffer from network latency, so compatible compute instances and networking matter. Independent tasks can often scale more simply because they communicate less. On the upper right, four storage icons show distinct access patterns: durable objects, shared file systems, block volumes and disposable local scratch. The correct storage choice depends on how workers read and write data. Now follow the lower-left S3 and FSx for Lustre diagram. FSx for Lustre can supply fast parallel file access and integrate with S3, but input staging, output persistence and data lifecycle still need explicit planning. The final panel compares managed batch scheduling and cluster tooling, such as ParallelCluster, for launching and operating compute jobs. Include queues, checkpoints and recovery, especially with interruptible capacity. A slow storage feed or inefficient communication can waste a powerful cluster. Align compute, inter-node networking, filesystem behavior and scheduler before claiming that adding nodes will improve completion time.

scenes.title: Auto Scaling groups: safe capacity bounds
scenes.visual_overview: The approved SAP slide diagrams auto scaling groups: safe capacity bounds in four numbered visual sections and a remember takeaway.
visual_walkthrough: Trace minimum, desired and maximum group capacity bounds on the left
Inspect AZ subnet selection and versioned launch-template deployment
Identify quota, capacity, launch and dependency failures that block desired health
Explain safe replacement, load balancing, state externalization and AZ resilience
scenes.visual_example: Review a production compute workload against the diagram and evaluate its concrete performance, security and failure requirements.
scenes.visual_synthesis: The architecture is appropriate only after its operational requirements, limits and failure response are validated.
scenes.narration: The central shield represents an Auto Scaling group's ongoing replacement and scaling process, but the four panels show why desired capacity is not a guarantee. Start at the upper-left scale: minimum, desired and maximum values define the group's operating bounds. Desired is a target number of instances, not proof that healthy capacity has actually launched. The upper-right panel shows supported subnets in multiple Availability Zones alongside a reproducible launch template. This enables the group to create consistent replacements where capacity is available. The lower-left warning illustrates quota limits, insufficient instance capacity, launch failures and broken dependencies. Any of these can prevent instances from reaching healthy service state. Finally, the lower-right panel makes the application design requirement explicit. Auto Scaling can launch replacement servers, but it cannot repair an application that stores its only copy of state on one failed host. Use suitable health checks, load balancing, independent state services and tested startup or warm-up behavior. Test an Availability Zone loss and verify the replacement capacity and dependent services survive. Treat desired capacity as the controller's goal, and measure actual healthy capacity before relying on availability claims.
